app.title: Ancient DNA Analyzer
app.summary: A person pastes a DNA sequence, uploads a FASTA file or loads demo sequences, and the sidebar lists each sequence with its length. A dashboard validates each sequence and shows its length, GC content, base ratios and ORF count, with tabs for base composition, GC skew along the sequence, a map of open reading frames and restriction cut sites. Further pages break the first sequence down by codon usage per reading frame, six-frame translation, candidate proteins above a chosen length, transcription and dinucleotide frequencies. The person can also pick a reference and a query sequence to count position-by-position differences split into transitions and transversions, and generate a short narrative summary of the statistics.

task.text: Profile DNA sequences by composition, coding features and cut sites, and count base differences between two of them.

data.text: One or more named DNA sequences from a FASTA file or a paste, and the statistics, features and differences computed from them.

stage.text: exploring DNA sequences once they are in hand, before deeper analysis such as alignment or species identification

mechanism.text: A sidebar holds the sequence input and switches between four pages; each page recomputes from the loaded sequences and shows metric cards above tabbed charts (composition radar, GC gauge, sliding-window heatmap, skew curve, ORF and restriction maps), with expanders listing the detail rows. Dropdowns for reading frame or reference and query sequence, and a protein length slider, rerun the calculations.

field.text: sequence composition and feature analysis in bioinformatics

workflow.name: profile sequences by computed statistics and features, and count differences between two

steps.here: paste a sequence with a name, upload a multi-record FASTA file, or load two demo sequences; the sidebar then lists each loaded sequence with its length in bp

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: each sequence is checked to contain only A, T, C or G, then gets metric cards for length, GC content (with its difference from 50%), AT/GC ratio, purine/pyrimidine ratio and ORF count

steps.step: look along each sequence for patterns and features
steps.here: tabs show a base composition radar, a GC gauge, a sliding-window nucleotide heatmap, windowed and cumulative GC skew, ORFs on all six frames drawn on a linear map, and restriction enzyme cut sites, with expanders listing positions

for the first sequence: codon usage and a codon bias score per chosen reading frame, six-frame translation, candidate proteins above a minimum length set by slider, RNA transcript, reverse complement and dinucleotide frequencies

pick a reference and a query sequence; both are cut to the shorter length and compared position by position, giving total mutations, mutation rate, transitions and transversions, a mutation plot and a table of differing positions
a button sends the statistics and the start of the sequence to a local language model for a short narrative, falling back to a rule-based summary from GC thresholds when no model is available

distinctive: every feature search runs on all six reading frames, three forward and three on the reverse complement
differences are counted by direct position-by-position comparison without alignment, so the two sequences are truncated to the shorter length
substitutions are classed as transitions or transversions, the split used to look for deamination damage in old DNA
codon usage is reported as relative synonymous codon usage, with an effective-number-of-codons bias score from 20 (extreme) to 61 (none)
restriction sites are found against a fixed built-in list of common enzymes
